title: Don’t cap opportunity: Maryland’s Heritage Areas create jobs and grow local economies
summary: Maryland's designated Heritage Areas preserve and inform our history while providing an economic return to their communities, but have been held back by a funding cap, writes Lucille Walker, who hopes passage of the "Lift the Cap" act this year can change that.
content:
by Lucille Walker, Maryland Matters April 18, 2026

by Lucille Walker, Maryland Matters April 18, 2026

At a time when our country often feels divided, Maryland has a unique program that invests in the places, stories, and traditions that bring people together. The Maryland Heritage Areas Program is a proven economic development engine that helps communities preserve their history while driving tourism, supporting small businesses and creating jobs.

Maryland is one of only two states in the nation with a comprehensive, state-based heritage area program, making it a national leader in using heritage as a tool for economic development.

For nearly 30 years, the program has been a quiet success story, delivering measurable results for communities from Western Maryland to the Eastern Shore. Today, Maryland’s 13 Heritage Areas generate $2.4 billion in annual economic activity and produce $319.8 million in state and local tax revenue each year. Every dollar invested in the program returns $7 directly to Maryland communities.

These investments benefit small businesses, Main Streets, historic sites, parks, trails, museums, waterfront and rural economic development, festivals and other tourism destinations that strengthen our state. They also support 40,000 jobs in Maryland, from museum staff to trail builders and festival organizers.

Despite this success, an outdated law has been holding the program back. Maryland’s Heritage Areas are currently limited by a $6 million statutory funding cap that no longer reflects today’s economic reality.

Inflation has increased project costs. Tourism demand has grown. Communities across the state have developed new projects ready to move forward. Yet the funding available to support those efforts has remained frozen.

The result is a widening gap between opportunity and capacity. In the most recent grant cycle, more than $12 million in eligible requests were submitted, more than double the program’s current funding capacity.

Fortunately, all that could change come July 1. Lawmakers this year passed the Maryland Heritage Area “Lift the Cap” legislation (HB 654 / SB 638), which removes this outdated barrier. Just as importantly, it does so without requiring new spending.

This bill does not appropriate funds, does not mandate spending and does not impact the current budget. Instead, it simply removes the outdated $6 million cap so that future funding decisions can be made through the normal legislative and budget process.

In other words, lifting the cap restores flexibility. It ensures that when Maryland is in a position to invest in a program that clearly works, we are not constrained by an outdated statute.

Across Maryland, communities are already demonstrating what greater investment can achieve.

In Southern Maryland, Heritage Area funding helped support the Commemorative to the Enslaved in St. Mary’s County, an artwork, poetry and history installation that honors the lives of people who were forced into slavery. This structure is located on the very site where an enslaved family’s cabin once stood.

Funding has also supported the preservation of Port Tobacco, once Maryland’s largest international seaport before the American Revolution. This area was home to communities within the larger Piscataway tribe for thousands of years.

And at the Calvert Marine Museum, heritage funding has helped develop exhibits that highlight the power of the Chesapeake Bay and illuminate a vanishing way of life tied to water and working waterfronts.

These projects preserve Maryland’s past while also driving real economic activity. Visitors come to experience these places, dine in local restaurants, stay in nearby hotels, shop in stores and attend festivals and events that strengthen community life.

That is the power of heritage tourism.

Other states are increasingly investing in place-based economic development strategies. Maryland should not fall behind, especially given the program’s already strong, proven results.

By lifting the cap on Heritage Area funding, Maryland can unlock opportunity, strengthen local economies, and ensure that the stories, landscapes, and communities that define our state continue to thrive for generations to come. It will allow Maryland to invest in economic development when resources allow.  Sometimes the smartest policy changes are also the simplest.
